It also serves to cement the mission’s design and industrial structure, both of which have undergone substantial changes over the last six years. In December 2020, ESA awarded an initial €86 million contract for the ClearSpace-1 mission to a consortium led by Swiss startup ClearSpace. At the time, the mission was expected to be launched in 2025 and remove a Vega payload adapter left in orbit following a launch in 2023. However, in August 2023, the adapter was struck by space debris, forcing a redesign and the selection of Proba-1 as the new target. In April 2024, ESA announced that OHB would take over leadership of the restructured project , with ClearSpace retaining responsibility for close-proximity and capture operations. The latest contract formalises OHB’s role as the project’s prime contractor for the implementation phase. The restructuring also appears to have prompted a change in how the mission will be launched. In May 2023, ClearSpace signed a contract with Arianespace to launch the ClearSpace-1 mission aboard a Vega C rocket in the second half of 2026. However, a technical paper presented at the 9th European Conference on Space Debris in April 2025 revealed that the mission would instead be launched aboard a dedicated microlauncher flight. candidates.raw_excerpt: NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft achieved another milestone this morning. Launched in 1977, it became the first human object to pass into interstellar space in August 2012 and is so far from Earth now that it takes one entire day for a radio signal to get there — one light-day. It also takes one light-day for Voyager 1 to send back the data it is still acquiring after all these decades. Voyager 1 passed the one light-day threshold at 5:16:07 am ET this morning at a distance of 16.094 billion miles (25.902 billion kilometers). That means it takes two days to communicate with Voyager — one day for the signal to get there and another day for the answer to come back. The spacecraft sent back stunning images of Jupiter in 1979 and Saturn in 1980. Since then it’s been on a quest to find whatever is out there beyond and report back to NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, CA. Its twin, Voyager 2, flew past Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune and also now is in interstellar space, but exited in a different direction. Voyager 1’s cameras were turned off to save power in February 1990 just after taking the iconic “Pale Blue Dot” image of Earth. The tiny dot in the middle of the gray streak is Earth as seen from a distance 3.7 billion miles (6 billion kilometers). However, the concept of sending a probe on a “Grand Tour” of the outer planets and eventually into interstellar space dates back to the 1960s. After a storied career exploring space, Voyager 1 deserves a look back at how it got to where it is today, and where it is going. NASA’s Voyager program The Voyager probes were conceived in the late 1960s and early 1970s as part of the larger Planetary Grand Tour program. This program would see probes fly past the outer planets of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune, Pluto (considered a planet until 2006), and Saturn’s moon, Titan. The probes would be able to fly past all the target planets via gravitational assists due to a planetary alignment that occurs only once every 175 years. The scientist who discovered this alignment, Gary Flandro, discovered the possibility in 1964. His calculations showed that the best option for the mission would be to launch spacecraft in 1977. The program would formally be endorsed by NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in 1966. The program would consist of four probes: two would fly past Jupiter, Saturn, and Pluto, and the other two would fly past Jupiter, Uranus, and Neptune. However, due to budget constraints from the upcoming Space Shuttle program, the Grand Tour program was shelved in December 1971. In 1972, the program would be scaled down to visit only four planets, with two probes built using hardware from the Mariner probes. The company ClearSpace has been working with ESA on the CS-1 mission since 2020. The goal of the mission is to demonstrate active debris removal with an object in orbit not designed to be captured. The mission originally planned to target a VESPA payload adapter left in orbit from a 2013 Vega launch, but that object was hit by debris in 2023 . candidates.raw_excerpt: On Nov. 18, 2013, NASA launched the MAVEN spacecraft to Mars. The name of NASA's MAVEN spacecraft stands for Mars Atmosphere and Volatile EvolutioN. The spacecraft was an orbiter designed to help scientists figure out what happened to the water on Mars and its atmosphere. Mars is dry today, but it data from several Mars missions suggest that it was a much wetter environment a long time ago. MAVEN tracked the rate of atmospheric loss from Mars . The planet has a super thin atmosphere that has been leaking into space for a few billion years. Scientists think that when Mars lost its atmosphere, water dried up on the surface as a result. Solar storms that blast radiation into the solar system appear to have blasted away some of the atmosphere. Carbon dioxide in the atmosphere once kept Mars warm enough to sustain liquid water on its surface , and losing that greenhouse gas turned Mars into a cold and dry place. An Atlas V rocket launches NASA's Mars MAVEN orbiter into space from Florida's Cape Canaveral Space Force Base on Nov. 18, 2013. After its launch in 2013, MAVEN spent about 10 months en route to Mars before entering orbit on Sept. 21, 2014 . candidates.title: Global patent filings hit record high in 2025, led by China
candidates.raw_excerpt:
Global patent applications reached a record 3.9 million in 2025, up 6% year on year and marking the fastest growth in nearly a decade, according to the World Intellectual Property Organization's World Intellectual Property Indicators report released on Wednesday. China ranked first by a wide margin.

Innovators based in China filed about 1.9 million patent applications, followed by the United States with 489,766, Japan with 466,301 and South Korea with 319,210.

Asia accounted for 71.2% of global patent filings in 2025, up from 61.9% in 2015. China's strong growth was the main driver, with the country accounting for about 68.5% of all applications filed in Asia.

In terms of technology fields, computer technology remained the largest area for patent applications in 2024, the latest year with complete data, accounting for 13% of published filings.

Energy storage, particularly batteries, was the largest category among green technology patent applications, accounting for 17.4%. Smart energy, grids and power transmission followed with 15.2%, while air pollution control accounted for 11.8%.

candidates.title: Chinese engineering body works to take its engineers global
candidates.raw_excerpt:
The Chinese Society of Engineers (CSE) is stepping up efforts to help Chinese engineers expand their international reach and promote openness, trust and cooperation within the global engineering community, the society said at a meeting on Tuesday to elect its new leadership.

In the next five years, the CSE aims to bring the total number of engineers meeting the international mutual recognition criteria to 7,000, secure mutual recognition of professional engineering qualifications for more than 500 engineers under bilateral arrangements, and train 10,000 engineers from developing countries, the meeting said.

Since its establishment five years ago, the society has carried out engineering competency assessments in 13 engineering technology fields. Its engineer members qualified for international mutual recognition have grown from just under 500 at the end of 2021 to nearly 4,000.

The CSE has also helped nearly 300 Chinese engineers gain recognition in China's Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, Myanmar, Singapore and the United Kingdom, obtaining overseas practicing qualifications or registered engineer titles from engineering institutions.

Meanwhile, more than 40 engineers from Myanmar, Singapore and Malaysia have become CSE engineer members through mutual recognition arrangements, marking a shift from one-way recognition of Chinese engineers overseas to a two-way process.

The society will focus on the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), Central Asia, the Middle East, South America and Africa, targeting fields where China has developed strong engineering capabilities. These include high-speed rail, ultra-high-voltage power transmission, information and communications, clean energy, and new energy vehicles.

If funding persisted, which it did, the hope was to bring Voyager 2 past Uranus and Neptune, taking advantage of a rare planetary alignment. Voyager 1, by contrast, made a turn at Saturn to look at the planet's rings and the prebiotic (pre-life-chemistry) moon of Titan , before flying outside the plane of the solar system. candidates.raw_excerpt: The failure of a Vulcan Centaur rocket carrying a full load of internet satellites for Amazon was caused by an anomaly in its first-stage booster, rocket maker United Launch Alliance said today (Nov. 17). That failure — which led to the loss of 40 Amazon Leo internet satellites — was recognized about 10 minutes after liftoff, but the problems began much earlier than that, ULA said in a statement. "While we appear to have lost telemetry and the mission at approximately 10 minutes into flight, early indications are that just after liftoff the launch vehicle experienced low booster performance, resulting in stage separation occurring when the vehicle was low in altitude and below minimal velocity to reach orbit," ULA wrote in today's update . The two-stage Vulcan Centaur is the successor to ULA's workhorse Atlas V rocket, which will retire after just six more flights. Vulcan debuted in January 2024 and now has a total of five launches under its belt. The new rocket has experienced problems on three of those missions. On both its second and fourth flights — which launched in October 2024 and February of this year, respectively — the nozzle of one of Vulcan's strap-on solid rocket boosters (SRBs) fell off about 30 seconds after liftoff. On both occasions, the rocket overcame the problem and successfully delivered its payloads to orbit. However, after the second occurrence, the U.S. Space Force paused national-security launches with Vulcan until ULA addressed the SRB nozzle issue. (The February 2026 flight was a Space Force mission.) That work led to "design and process improvements to the nozzle," ULA said in an Oct. 28 update . And those tweaks apparently worked. "All indications are that the solid rocket booster performance was nominal, following nozzle improvements implemented for this launch," the company wrote in today's update. candidates.title: ULA Vulcan Anomaly Has Pentagon Implications
candidates.raw_excerpt: One of the Pentagon’s two workhorses to orbit just got grounded—for the second time this year. ULA’s Vulcan rocket lifted off Sunday on its first mission for Amazon Leo, carrying 40 satellites onboard. However, an anomaly early in the flight resulted in the loss of all the satellites, triggering an FAA mishap investigation.  “ULA exists to provide assured access to space for our nation and for the customers who depend on us,” the company wrote in a statement on X. “That purpose is why we take on some of the hardest missions in spaceflight, and why we hold ourselves to the standard of mission success. Today, we did not meet that standard.” The company announced Tuesday morning that the mission was lost 10 minutes into the flight, but that the problems started just after liftoff. Problems with the booster performance resulted in stage separation occurring when the rocket was moving too slow to reach orbit, resulting in the failure. A look back: It’s the second problem faced by Vulcan this year. In February, a Vulcan launch faced issues with one of the rocket’s solid-rocket boosters, though Vulcan was able to deliver its Space Force SSA payloads into orbit. ULA confirmed that the solid rocket boosters on Sunday’s flight performed nominally. Despite the successful deployment, the February mission still forced a nine-month grounding of the rocket while the Space Force investigated the problems. In October, the Space Force announced it had reassigned six national-security launches to SpaceX during the grounding.  Vulcan returned to flight on Sunday, only to immediately suffer another, more serious issue.  The NSS-Elephant in the room: The Pentagon’s National Security Space Launch program includes two lanes to get defense payloads into orbit: Lane 1 includes less complicated missions that can accept more risk. candidates.title: On this day in space! Nov. 17, 1967: NASA's Surveyor 6 moon probe makes 1st-ever successful launch and hop from the lunar surface
candidates.raw_excerpt: On Nov. 17, 1967, NASA's Surveyor 6 spacecraft made the first liftoff from the lunar surface. Surveyor 6 was one of several robotic lunar missions NASA sent to scout the moon before sending humans there. It took television pictures of the surface and learned about the composition of lunar soil. Then came the big liftoff. First Surveyor 6 launched from the surface and hopped to another position about 8 feet (2 meters) away. Next, Surveyor 6 took pictures of its original landing site. Flight controllers on Earth could see the landing pad prints of Surveyor 6. They also saw an imprint from the rocket exhaust when Surveyor 6 lifted off. Surveyor 6 showed that spacecraft could land on the moon, and lift off again. Less than two years later, humans did the same thing during Apollo 11 . A panorama of the moon from NASA's Surveyor 6 moon lander in November 1967. (Image credit: NASA/GSFC/LROC) Why it mattered NASA's Surveyor 6 spacecraft launched to the moon on Nov. 7, 1967 and made its first landing on the lunar surface on Nov. 10 of that year. It's primary mission was to make a soft landing on the moon in the Sinus Medii of the moon. The probe took nearly 30,000 photos of the moon during its 16 days on the lunar surface, with the lander shutting down due to the onset of lunar night on Nov. 26. Surveyor 6 was the sixth and penultimate moon mission of NASA's Surveyor lunar program, so a lot of what it did (launching and landing on the moon ) had been done before. But a lunar liftoff? That was something new. This Boeing diagram depicts the short launch and hop on the moon by NASA's Surveyor 6 moon lander on Nov. 17, 1967. candidates.title: NASA wants you to 'shine bright' today for Voyager 1's light-day milestone. Here's how
candidates.raw_excerpt: As NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft prepares to reach a historic distance from Earth, the agency is inviting people around the world to celebrate by shining a light into the night sky in honor of humanity's farthest-flung spacecraft. The event, called "Shine Bright for Voyager's Light-Day," will take place after sunset on Tuesday (Nov. 17), the day before Voyager 1 gets one light-day from Earth . And that's a big milestone: One light-day is the distance light travels in a day — about 16 billion miles (26 billion kilometers). NASA is encouraging "Shine Bright" participants to create a symbolic wave of golden light around the planet by flashing the spacecraft's three-letter mission call sign, VGR, in Morse code, according to a statement from the space agency. To celebrate the spacecraft, participants can use a flashlight, phone, bike light or other portable light source to send the signal skyward. And don't fret if you're unfamiliar with Morse code : NASA has created an automated flasher that can be opened in a smartphone or tablet browser to display the VGR sequence. The spacecraft’s call sign pattern consists of three quick flashes followed by one long flash for the letter V, two long flashes and one quick flash for G, and one quick flash, one long flash and another quick flash for R. Participants are encouraged to repeat the sequence for about a minute, NASA officials said. The three-letter call sign for NASA's Voyager mission, VGR, spelled out in Morse code. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) NASA also invites people to photograph or record their light signals and share them on social media, tagging the agency's official account, @NASA. The goal is to create a worldwide display of light marking a milestone nearly five decades in the making. The celebration is intended as a symbolic tribute rather than an actual attempt to communicate with Voyager 1 . candidates.title: The NSA’s Internal Computer System for Sharing Highly Classified Information Just Went Down
candidates.raw_excerpt: November has been marked by a series of severe computing outages. Several of Microsoft’s widely-used online services went down, causing major disruptions across offices worldwide. Then, the Federal Aviation Administration shut down all air travel across the US without notice on Friday, leaving countless passengers stranded and confused. This week, the IT headache of major proportions continued, with almost every major bank in the country reeling from outages affecting online services. Now, even the National Security Agency’s in-house communications network has gone down, inside sources told CNN . The incident could have some hair-raising implications because government employees use the network, dubbed NSA Net, to communicate classified information with each other internally. CNN ’s sources said there was no evidence of a cyberattack, echoing a refrain in the month’s other major outages. The NSA has yet to publicly comment on the matter. Whether AI is to blame for the continuing interruptions remains a major subject of debate. We know that AI-generated code frequently includes errors that can easily go overlooked as managers push employees to use the tech at all costs. However, representatives at Microsoft and the FAA maintain that AI had nothing to do with the outages. Not everybody agrees with that sentiment. During a controversial appearance on Fox News on Monday , Homeland Security secretary Markwayne Mullin said that he had “talked to one guy in the tech industry,” who told him AI was to blame after all, with software that isn’t “designed to work as fast” as AI causing a “ripple effect.” Whether Mullin’s mystery tech “guy” insider will eventually be proven right remains to be seen.
